processing: A part-baked, part-pan-fired tender green: spread to wilt, fixed, cooled, rolled and shaped, then dried. The method reportedly derives from Mengding tea and yellow bud tea.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for tender Zhejiang greens; the picks keep the leaf stalk and fish leaf attached.
appearance_dry: Short, stout, whole yellow-green shoots, opening like orchids, with golden fish leaves and faintly reddish stalk ends.
appearance_wet: Whole shoots, green tinged with yellow.
taste_profile: Known for a clear, high and quiet fragrance rather than force; the cup is clean and light.

brewing.notes: A glass lets you see the whole shoots. Short of that, use a wide cup and cooled water.

vintage_note: As with other Zhejiang famous greens it is sold as the current spring harvest and is best fresh, within the year. Provincial and group standards grade it by level, so look for a stated grade and the Jiande origin.
description:
Jiande Bao Cha, also called Yanzhou Bao Cha after the old name of the area, is a small speciality green from Jiande, west of Hangzhou. Its name comes from the shape: compact whole shoots that look like buds about to open, classed among orchid-shaped teas.

It keeps more of the shoot than most greens, stalk and fish leaf included. That is the identifying mark: the little fish leaf turns golden and the stalk end faintly red against a yellow-green shoot. Part baking and part pan-firing keeps the shape whole.

The fragrance is its strength: clear, high and quiet. Tasting notes beyond that are few, and the cup is generally described as clean rather than heavy, as is typical of tender Zhejiang greens. Cool water and a clear glass show it at its best.

The tea is little known abroad, and good lots mostly stay local. When you find it, look at the leaf: a fish leaf and reddish stalk end are what set it apart from generic Zhejiang green.
history:
Accounts date its creation to 1870, in the Sandu Xiaolibu and Meicheng Dongguan area of Jiande, and say the method was drawn from Sichuan's Mengding tea and Anhui's yellow bud tea. It was originally counted as a yellow tea before being classed as green as the process changed.

In May 2008 the national quality authority approved geographical indication protection, and a Jiande group standard followed in 2018. The city still promotes it with spring festivals, including one reported in April 2025.
